content: 1. The recommended dosage of kanamycin is 5 mg/kg per dose, administered every 8 to 12 hours. The total daily dose should not exceed 15 mg/kg. For intramuscular (IM) administration, the dose should be divided into equal intervals every 12 hours. If continuously high blood levels are desired, a daily dose of 15 mg/kg may be divided and administered every 6 to 8 hours. 2. For aerosolized administration, 250 mg of kanamycin can be given every 6 to 12 hours via nebulization. 3. In patients with a creatinine clearance (CrCl) of 50–80 mL/min, administer 60–90% of the usual dose or adjust the dosing interval to every 8–12 hours. For CrCl of 10–50 mL/min, administer 30–70% of the usual dose or adjust the dosing interval to every 12 hours. For CrCl <10 mL/min, administer 20–30% of the usual dose or adjust the dosing interval to every 24–48 hours. 4. Therapeutic drug monitoring is essential. The target peak serum concentration is 15–30 mg/L, and the trough concentration is 5–10 mg/L. 5. Kanamycin decreases the efficacy of oral microbiota products due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid co-administration or consider alternative therapies. Oral microbiota products contain bacterial spores, and their efficacy may be reduced when co-administered with antibacterial agents. Complete the antibiotic regimen 2–4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. 6. Cephalosporins, such as cefaclor, cefadroxil, cefazolin, cefdinir, cefditoren, cefepime, cefiderocol, cefixime, cefotaxime, cefotetan, cefoxitin, cefpirome, cefpodoxime, cefprozil, ceftaroline, ceftazidime, ceftibuten, ceftizoxime, ceftobiprole, and ceftolozane/tazobactam, increase the nephrotoxic and/or ototoxic effects of kanamycin. Use caution and monitor closely when co-administering these drugs. Cephalosporins may enhance the nephrotoxic effects of aminoglycosides. 7. Levo-ketoconazole increases kanamycin levels or effects by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor closely. Conversely, levo-ketoconazole may also decrease kanamycin levels through an unknown mechanism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is advised. 8. Magnesium sulfate/potassium chloride and sodium sulfate/potassium sulfate/magnesium sulfate increase the toxicity of kanamycin by causing fluid and electrolyte abnormalities. These abnormalities may increase the risk of adverse events such as seizures, arrhythmias, and renal impairment. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Voclosporin and kanamycin may mutually increase each other's toxicity through nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Modify therapy and monitor closely. Co-administration with drugs associated with nephrotoxicity may increase the risk of acute and/or chronic nephrotoxicity. 10. Kanamycin enhances the anticoagulant effects of warfarin. Use caution and monitor closely. 11. Co-administration of kanamycin and entecavir may increase the effects of either drug by reducing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is minor or unknown, but close monitoring is recommended. Drugs that reduce renal function or compete for active tubular secretion may increase serum concentrations of either entecavir or kanamycin. 12. Neurotoxicity, manifested as bilateral auditory and vestibular ototoxicity, can occur in patients with pre-existing renal damage or in those treated with higher doses or for longer durations than recommended. High-frequency hearing loss typically occurs first and may only be detected through audiometric testing. Vertigo may also occur, indicating vestibular injury. 13. Aminoglycosides, including kanamycin, are potentially nephrotoxic. The risk is higher in patients with impaired renal function and in those receiving high doses or prolonged therapy. Rarely, nephrotoxicity may not become apparent until a few days after therapy cessation. 14. Use kanamycin with caution in premature infants and neonates due to renal immaturity, which prolongs the serum half-life of the drug. 15. Neuromuscular blockade and respiratory paralysis have been reported following parenteral injection, topical instillation (e.g., orthopedic or abdominal irrigation), or oral use of aminoglycosides, especially when administered soon after anesthesia or muscle relaxants. If blockade occurs, calcium salts may reverse the effects, but mechanical respiratory assistance may be necessary. 16. Avoid concurrent or sequential use of neurotoxic and/or nephrotoxic drugs, including other aminoglycosides (e.g., amikacin, streptomycin, neomycin, gentamicin, and puromycin), to minimize the risk of cumulative toxicity.
